commonMistakes.title: Reversing Markup to Find Original
commonMistakes.description: If a $100 item is discounted by 20% to $80, adding 20% of $80 does not recover $100 ($80 + $16 = $96). Always divide by the remaining decimal factor (1 - Rate).

commonMistakes.title: Confusing Proportions with Multipliers
commonMistakes.description: Multiplying a number by 20% means finding one-fifth of that number. To increase a number by 20%, multiply by 1.20, not 0.20.

commonMistakes.title: Dividing by Zero
commonMistakes.description: When determining what percentage X is of Y, the denominator Y cannot be zero. Zero represents an empty whole, making the percentage ratio undefined.

faqs.q: What is the formula to calculate a percentage of a number?
faqs.a: To find X% of Y, divide the percentage X by 100 to convert it into a decimal rate, then multiply by the total number Y. Mathematically: Result = (X ÷ 100) × Y. For example, 15% of 200 is (15 ÷ 100) × 200 = 30.

faqs.q: How do I calculate what percentage one number is of another?
faqs.a: Divide the partial amount (X) by the total baseline amount (Y) and multiply the quotient by 100: Percentage = (X ÷ Y) × 100. For instance, if you scored 45 out of 50 on a quiz, your percentage score is (45 ÷ 50) × 100 = 90%.

faqs.q: How do you find the original price before a discount?
faqs.a: To recover the original value after a discount, divide the sale price by (1 minus the discount rate as a decimal). If an item costs $80 after a 20% discount: Original Price = $80 ÷ (1 - 0.20) = $80 ÷ 0.80 = $100.

faqs.q: How do you find the original price before sales tax or markup?
faqs.a: Divide the final price by (1 plus the tax or markup rate as a decimal). If a total receipt is $108 with an 8% sales tax included: Pre-tax Original = $108 ÷ (1 + 0.08) = $108 ÷ 1.08 = $100.

faqs.q: How does this tool differ from the Percentage Change Calculator?
faqs.a: This Percentage Calculator solves direct proportions, base rates, and reverse percentage recovery. To calculate the historical relative increase or decrease between two distinct baseline values, use our dedicated Percentage Change Calculator.

faqs.q: Can a percentage calculation result in a number greater than 100%?
faqs.a: Yes. When the part value (X) is greater than the whole value (Y), the percentage will exceed 100%. For example, 150 is 150% of 100, which commonly occurs in growth metrics and sales quotas.
Direct percentages have an interesting symmetry: X% of Y is always mathematically identical to Y% of X. For example, 8% of 50 is 4, and 50% of 8 is also 4.
